text: Reproductive strategies in solitary carnivores are expected to vary between males and females. In these species, males are commonly polygynous and often significantly larger than females. Males are thought to compete with other males for territories that encompass the home ranges of multiple females and are believed to attempt to mate with every reproductive female residing within their territory [ 4 , 7 , 8 , 10 , 11 ]. Conversely, female solitary carnivores tend to overlap with few potential mates [ 8 , 12 , 13 ], and may primarily rely on carefully assessing cues to select a mate that best enhances survival of their offspring [ 2 ]. A key aspect of female mate selection is thought to be the body mass of potential mates. Larger mass in male carnivores appears to be selected for across generations as an indicator of greater fitness and physical dominance, both of which can be expressed via larger territories [ 8 , 9 ]. However, recent advances in our understanding of mate selection suggest that female selection is more complex than simplistic assessments of male ornamentation or mass [ 9 ].
source_label: The Role of Scent Marking in Mate Selection by Female Pumas ( Puma concolor )
